The central question is whether INT4 quantization errors distribute uniformly across all attention heads, or whether heads that carry disproportionate weight in downstream task performance (importance-tier-1 heads) accumulate error differently than expendable heads — and whether that asymmetry compounds in ways that standard per-tensor or per-channel calibration statistics fail to detect. Key concepts include: the non-linear sensitivity of weight quantization to outlier activation magnitudes (a head with rare but large activations will incur clipping error that average-based calibration systematically underestimates); the importance tiering of heads, which is typically measured by gradient-based attribution or pruning ablation scores; and error accumulation, meaning that quantization noise in early layers feeds into the key/query dot-products of later layers, so heads that aggregate information across many tokens act as error amplifiers rather than error sinks.

What a beginner misses is that calibration datasets create a false sense of security: a head may look well-quantized on the calibration distribution but catastrophically degrade on out-of-distribution inputs precisely because it was important enough to develop sharp, rare activation peaks that the calibration set never triggered. The expert worry is therefore not average quantization error (which looks fine in benchmarks) but the covariance between a head's importance tier and the skewness of its weight/activation distribution — high-importance heads are often high-skewness heads, meaning the very heads you can least afford to corrupt are the ones where INT4's 16-level resolution is most inadequate.

subject: Quantization error accumulation asymmetry across attention head importance tiers in post-training INT4 compression
prompt:
Given that importance-tier-1 heads tend to have high-skewness activation distributions, what specific property of INT4's quantization grid makes clipping error on those heads categorically worse than rounding error — and why does that distinction matter for choosing a mitigation strategy?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-2507)
response:
INT4's quantization grid has only 16 representable levels, so the scale factor that maps the full floating-point range onto those 16 levels is determined by the tensor's maximum (or a percentile of it) — and this is where clipping versus rounding diverge categorically. Rounding error is bounded: for a given scale, every value lands within ±0.5 LSB (least significant bit) of the nearest grid point, which for INT4 is at most 1/32nd of the full-scale range — a small, zero-mean, roughly uniform noise that tends to cancel across many weights. Clipping error has no such bound and is systematically one-signed: when a high-skewness head produces an outlier activation at, say, 6σ while the scale was fit to the 99th percentile at 3σ, that outlier is hard-clipped to the grid maximum and the error is the full difference — potentially 50–100% of the true value — with no cancellation because all clipped values err in the same direction. This asymmetry is precisely what SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2022) was designed to address: they observed that in LLaMA-class models, fewer than 0.1% of activation values account for the majority of quantization error, and those values are always outliers in specific channels tied to specific heads, not random noise. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2022) sidesteps this partially by solving a layer-wise reconstruction problem that absorbs some clipping error back into the weights, but it cannot recover information that has been hard-clipped to zero gradient — once you're outside the grid, the Hessian-weighted update has nothing to work with. The mitigation distinction matters because rounding error calls for finer grids or stochastic rounding (statistical fixes), while clipping error calls for range-reshaping before quantization — either activation migration (SmoothQuant), rotation-based outlier suppression (QuaRot, 2024), or simply assigning higher-bit budgets to tier-1 heads, which mixed-precision schemes like LLM.int8() pioneered but INT4 frameworks have been slow to extend.

SmoothQuant's migration works by dividing activation channels by a per-channel smoothing factor s and multiplying the corresponding weight rows by s, keeping the mathematical product invariant — but this assumes the weight matrix has headroom to absorb the scaling without itself hitting INT4's clipping boundary. For importance-tier-1 heads, this assumption frequently breaks: these heads tend to have weights that are already large in magnitude because they've been pushed during training to amplify specific attention patterns (induction heads, for instance, develop sharp, high-magnitude key projection weights to implement prefix matching), so multiplying by s > 1 pushes already-large weight values past the INT4 scale threshold, trading an activation clipping problem for a weight clipping problem without net gain. The failure mode is a "whack-a-mole" dynamic that Ashkboos et al. (QuaRot, 2024) explicitly characterize: when both the activation and weight distributions are heavy-tailed in the same projection, no scalar per-channel migration factor can simultaneously bring both within INT4 range, because the product constraint means shrinking one distribution's effective range forces the other to expand. In practice this shows up as a non-monotonic relationship between the smoothing factor α (SmoothQuant's interpolation hyperparameter between 0 and 1) and downstream perplexity for specific heads: for most heads, sweeping α from 0.5 to 0.85 monotonically reduces error, but for tier-1 heads in models like LLaMA-2-70B, perplexity curves develop a local minimum at low α values and then worsen again, a signature that weight-side clipping has become the dominant error source. The deeper issue is that per-channel scalar smoothing is a rank-1 intervention on what is fundamentally a rank-k outlier structure — real outlier activations in high-importance heads tend to co-occur across multiple channels simultaneously (they're driven by specific token types, not independent channel noise), so a diagonal rescaling cannot rotate the joint distribution into a quantization-friendly shape. This is precisely the motivation for rotation-based methods like QuaRot and SpinQuant, which apply orthogonal transformations to spread outlier energy across all dimensions rather than migrating it between activation and weight sides — but those methods introduce their own failure mode for tier-1 heads that warrants careful examination.

When QuaRot applies orthogonal rotation R to the Q projection and the same R to the K projection, the attention score Q·Kᵀ is preserved exactly in full precision — R·Q and R·K cancel in the dot product — but this invariance shatters the moment either Q or K is quantized independently after rotation, because the quantization error in R·Q and the quantization error in R·K no longer cancel; instead they interact multiplicatively in the dot product, producing correlated error whose magnitude scales with the head dimension d_k. The geometric structure that makes a tier-1 head important is typically a small number of privileged directions in the Q/K space — for induction heads, the query vector needs to align precisely with a specific key subspace corresponding to previous token positions, and this alignment is implemented as a low-rank geometric relationship (Elhage et al., 2021 mechanistic interpretability work shows these structures live in rank-1 to rank-3 subspaces of the full 64- or 128-dimensional head space). A rotation R chosen to minimize weight quantization error — typically via a random Hadamard matrix in QuaRot, or a learned rotation in SpinQuant — will generically mix those privileged low-rank directions with all other dimensions, spreading the functionally critical subspace across the entire rotated basis; after INT4 quantization, the reconstruction error projects back onto those privileged directions and corrupts precisely the geometric relationship the head depends on. The practical signature is that rotation-based methods show disproportionate degradation on tasks requiring precise positional or syntactic attention patterns — needle-in-haystack retrieval and long-range coreference — even when aggregate perplexity looks acceptable, because perplexity averages over all heads while these tasks route almost entirely through tier-1 heads. SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2024) partially mitigates this by learning R through a Cayley manifold optimization that minimizes quantization error on calibration data, but if the calibration set doesn't contain examples that activate the tier-1 head's privileged subspace, the learned rotation has no gradient signal to preserve that subspace and will sacrifice it for gains on the majority of heads. The core tension is that the rotation which equalizes singular values of the weight matrix (ideal for quantization) is in direct conflict with the rotation that preserves the low-rank geometric structure of functional importance — these are opposite objectives, and no single orthogonal transformation can simultaneously achieve both for a head whose importance derives from anisotropy.

The decomposition you're describing — W = W_low + W_residual where W_low = UΣVᵀ truncated to rank r and kept in FP16, while W_residual is INT4 — is exactly the architecture explored in LoftQ (Liu et al., 2023) and partially in AQLM (Egiazarian et al., 2024), and it works cleanly for linear layers in isolation. The surgical appeal is real: for a Q projection whose functional importance lives in a rank-2 subspace, you'd retain perhaps 2×128×2 = 512 FP16 parameters versus 128×128 = 16,384 INT4 parameters, a negligible precision budget that protects the geometrically critical directions. The first thing that breaks is the key-side symmetry: protecting W_Q's functional subspace in FP16 does nothing for W_K's corresponding subspace unless you apply a matched decomposition there too, and the functional subspaces of Q and K are not independently defined — the rank-2 Q subspace is only meaningful relative to the rank-2 K subspace it's designed to align with, so you need coordinated low-rank protection across both projections simultaneously, which doubles the bookkeeping and requires that the SVD decompositions be computed jointly rather than independently. The second failure is more fundamental: the attention score is (W_low_Q + W_res_Q)x · (W_low_K + W_res_K)x, which expands into four cross terms, and the interaction term W_res_Q·x · W_low_K·x couples INT4 quantization noise from the residual Q component directly into the protected K subspace — there's no way to eliminate this cross-contamination without zeroing out the residual entirely in those directions, which defeats the compression. The third problem is the value projection W_V: even if Q and K are perfectly protected, the attention weights they produce are applied to V·x, and if W_V is INT4-quantized without analogous low-rank protection, the tier-1 head's correctly computed attention pattern is selecting over a corrupted value space, so the functional subspace protection in Q/K yields no downstream benefit unless the V projection is also treated — and now your "surgical" intervention has metastasized to three matrices per head. What LoftQ finds empirically is that the alternating optimization between low-rank component and quantized residual converges to different solutions depending on initialization order, suggesting the loss landscape has multiple local minima where the low-rank component captures different subspaces, and there's no guarantee the SVD-initialized solution captures the functionally important subspace rather than merely the highest-variance one — which for tier-1 heads may not be the same thing.

The functional subspace could in principle be identified by several signals: activation patching (isolating which directions in Q/K space, when ablated, maximally degrade task performance), causal tracing as in Meng et al.'s ROME work (2022), or direct probing of the head's output subspace across a task-stratified corpus. Gradient-based attribution — the obvious answer — is self-defeating for a specific structural reason: the gradient of task loss with respect to W_Q measures sensitivity at the current weight values, but post-training quantization changes those values, so the pre-quantization gradient identifies directions important to the full-precision model, not directions that will remain important or recoverable after the INT4 residual introduces its correlated noise; you're optimizing the decomposition for a model that no longer exists after compression. A subtler problem is that gradient magnitude conflates two distinct phenomena — directions where the model is sensitive because they're functionally critical, and directions where the model is sensitive because the loss landscape is locally steep due to near-cancellation between components, the latter being an artifact of how the weights settled during training rather than a signal of functional importance. Activation patching is more honest because it directly measures the counterfactual: replace the head's output in a specific subspace with its mean value and measure task degradation, which is exactly what Conmy et al.'s ACDC (2023) does at the circuit level and what you'd want to do at the subspace level — but this requires a task-specific evaluation set with enough examples to estimate the patching effect reliably, and the result is subspace-importance scores that are dataset-conditional, not universal. The practical answer used implicitly in some structured pruning work (e.g., Sheared LLaMA, Xia et al., 2023) is to use Fisher information estimated from a diverse held-out corpus as a proxy — the Fisher diagonal identifies directions where small perturbations produce large expected loss changes across many inputs, which is more robust than single-task gradients — but Fisher estimation for a full attention head's Q/K subspace requires storing and averaging outer products of gradients, which is memory-prohibitive at 70B scale without further approximation. The deepest problem is that functional subspace identification and quantization-robust subspace identification are asking different questions: the former asks which directions matter for the task, the latter asks which directions can survive INT4 noise without destroying the Q/K alignment — and a direction can be simultaneously functionally critical and quantization-fragile, meaning no decomposition strategy can protect it without keeping it entirely in high precision, collapsing back to the question of which heads to exempt from INT4 entirely.

The empirical answer is yes — query vectors for tier-1 heads do cluster discretely, and this has been documented concretely: Schlag et al. (2021) and subsequent mechanistic interpretability work show that induction heads operate with query vectors that fall into essentially two modes (a "searching" mode triggered by the current token and a "copying" mode triggered by positional context), while Olsson et al. (2022) demonstrate that the full behavioral repertoire of an induction head is captured by a rank-2 subspace of the QK circuit. This clustering is not an artifact of the corpus — it reflects the discrete nature of the computational primitive the head implements, which means the cluster centroids are corpus-stable in a way that gradient attribution is not, making them a genuinely more robust signal for subspace identification. The centroid-as-basis idea is sound in principle: running k-means with k=3 to k=8 on query vectors collected across a large diverse corpus, then using the top principal components of the centroid matrix as the protected subspace basis, would give you a data-driven low-rank basis that reflects the head's actual operational modes rather than its weight variance structure. The failure mode is quantization-specific: the cluster centroids define the subspace that the full-precision model uses, but after INT4 quantization of the residual W_residual component, the effective query vectors shift — the centroid geometry is measured on the pre-quantization model, so the protected subspace is calibrated to a distribution of query vectors that the quantized model will no longer produce, creating a mismatch between the protected basis and the actual post-quantization query trajectory. A second problem is that clustering operates on the output of W_Q applied to input tokens, meaning the clusters conflate the subspace structure of W_Q itself with the input token distribution — a head might appear to have 3 query modes because the input corpus has 3 token types that activate it, not because W_Q has rank-3 structure, and protecting the centroid subspace in that case protects an input-distribution artifact rather than a weight-space geometric primitive. The strongest version of this approach would combine centroid identification with a perturbation test: for each candidate basis vector, measure whether small rotations away from it produce disproportionate attention pattern degradation across diverse inputs, filtering out corpus-driven pseudo-modes and retaining only the directions where the head's geometry is genuinely brittle.

Diffuse attention heads — what Elhage et al. (2021) call "uniform" heads and what shows up empirically as heads with near-constant attention entropy across token positions — are precisely the case where clustering breaks down completely, because their query vectors don't cluster at all; they're approximately isotropic in the query space, meaning the head is computing something closer to a weighted average over all positions than a pattern-specific retrieval. These heads exist and are functionally important in a categorically different way: rather than implementing sharp computational primitives like induction or previous-token lookup, they act as low-pass filters or context smoothers that aggregate broad distributional information, and their importance shows up not in ablation of specific attention patterns but in degradation of the residual stream's "background" representation quality when they're removed. Quantization error manifests oppositely in diffuse versus sharp heads: for a sharp head, the dominant failure mode is the destruction of the precise Q/K alignment in a low-rank subspace (the needle-in-haystack problem), while for a diffuse head, no single direction is privileged, so INT4 rounding error averages out across the attention distribution — the head is naturally robust to quantization noise because diffuse attention is essentially computing a sum where individual term errors cancel. This means the importance-tier asymmetry we've been tracking runs in a surprising direction for diffuse heads: they may be high-importance by ablation metrics (removing them hurts perplexity significantly) yet low-sensitivity to INT4 quantization, because their function is implemented redundantly across many dimensions rather than concentrated in a fragile low-rank subspace. The concrete implication is that a mixed-precision budget allocation scheme that assigns higher bit-width based solely on ablation importance scores will misallocate precision — it will waste high-precision budget on diffuse heads that don't need it and potentially under-protect sharp tier-1 heads, unless the allocation signal distinguishes between importance-via-concentration (sharp heads, quantization-fragile) and importance-via-breadth (diffuse heads, quantization-robust). Voita et al. (2019) showed that heads can be pruned in clusters with minimal loss, and the heads that survive pruning longest are disproportionately the sharp, pattern-specific ones — which retroactively suggests that diffuse heads are both more redundant and more quantization-tolerant, a double signal that current INT4 frameworks ignore entirely when making per-head precision decisions.
